passage:
At the lunch table in their school in Manchester, Siddiq leaned forward. "Yesterday at the park there were a hundred dogs. A HUNDRED. And one was as big as a horse, and it chose me to throw the ball."
Kofi stopped chewing. "A hundred? Did you count?"
Siddiq waved his sandwich. "Maybe not exactly. Loads, though. At least twenty." He grinned. "Okay, seven. But the big one was really big."
Everyone laughed, and Siddiq laughed too, his ears pink. At home he told his gran, and this time there were twelve dogs. She raised an eyebrow. "Twelve?" "Seven," he said, "but twelve sounds better." She laughed and asked which one he liked best.

qa.q: How many dogs did Siddiq finally admit he saw?
qa.a: Siddiq admitted, "Okay, seven."

qa.q: Why did Siddiq say there were a hundred dogs?
qa.a: He wanted the story to be exciting and to be noticed; leaning forward and grinning, he was enjoying the attention more than trying to fool anyone.

qa.q: What small step could help Siddiq enjoy telling stories without stretching them?
qa.a: He could tell the true number and put the excitement into the details, like the huge dog that chose him, which was already a good story.

qa.q: How might Kofi see Siddiq's changing numbers?
qa.a: Kofi seems to find it funny rather than feel fooled, since Siddiq quickly admitted the real number and everyone laughed together.

grounding: A boy turns seven dogs into a hundred to make his story exciting and win attention, as play rather than a plan to deceive.

passage:
Monday circle time in Class 3B. Madhuri Ma'am asked who had news. Vaibhav's hand shot up. "I scored the winning goal in the house match! From the middle of the field!"
A boy near the window frowned. "You didn't. You passed, and someone else scored."
Vaibhav's cheeks went red. He looked at his shoes. "I kind of helped," he mumbled.
Madhuri Ma'am didn't call it a lie. "Tell us about the pass," she said. "Where were you standing?" Slowly Vaibhav described running down the left side, seeing the space, and kicking it across. His voice got louder as he went. "That's a proper assist," Ma'am said. The class clapped, and Vaibhav sat down grinning, this time about something real.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav first claim at circle time?
qa.a: Vaibhav claimed he scored the winning goal in the house match, from the middle of the field.

qa.q: Why do you think Vaibhav looked at his shoes when he was corrected?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed that his bigger story was caught, since he had wanted the class to be impressed.

qa.q: How did Madhuri Ma'am turn the moment around?
qa.a: She didn't call it a lie but asked about his pass, so Vaibhav could feel proud of what really happened.

qa.q: How might the boy near the window feel about Vaibhav's claim?
qa.a: He may feel it was unfair for Vaibhav to take credit for a goal someone else scored, which is why he spoke up.

grounding: A boy stretches his part in a match into the winning goal to feel important, and a teacher helps him find pride in the true story.

passage:
I'm Parveen, and when I was nine, our class went on a trip to the hill fort. That evening I told everyone in my building, "There were a HUNDRED monkeys! One stole Mridul's sandwich and ran up the wall!"
The little kids gasped. Even the watchman laughed. I felt like the most exciting person in the whole colony.
Then Mridul came down with his cricket bat and said, "It was six monkeys. And it stole a banana."
Everyone looked at me. My face went hot. I said, "It felt like a hundred!" and ran upstairs.
Later, Ammi asked why I was sulking. I told her. She laughed kindly and said, "You wanted them to feel how exciting it was. Next time, say 'so many monkeys, it felt like a hundred.' Then it's a story, not a trick."
I still say that now.

qa.q: How many monkeys did Mridul say there were?
qa.a: It was six monkeys.

qa.q: Why did Parveen's face go hot when Mridul spoke?
qa.a: Parveen felt embarrassed, because the exciting story had been exposed in front of everyone who had just been listening.

qa.q: What did Ammi suggest Parveen could say next time?
qa.a: Ammi suggested saying "so many monkeys, it felt like a hundred," so the story stays exciting without tricking anyone.

qa.q: How might Mridul have felt hearing the hundred-monkey story?
qa.a: Mridul may have felt a bit annoyed or left out, since he was there and knew it wasn't true, and his banana became a sandwich.

grounding: It shows a child stretching a trip story to win attention, more from play and wanting to matter than from a plan to fool anyone.

passage:
Class 4B, teacher's notes, Monday.
In our news circle, Noor stood up and announced that she scored the winning goal in Saturday's football match. The class cheered. Then Chaitanya, who plays in the same team, said quietly, "I scored it. Noor passed to me."
Noor's ears went red. She said, "Well, I nearly scored it."
I didn't correct her in front of everyone. After the circle, I asked Noor to help me tidy the reading corner and asked what the best moment of the match was for her. She said, "When I passed and everyone shouted."
I told her that pass sounds like a proud moment all by itself. She thought about it and then went to Chaitanya and said, "Your goal was good." He grinned.
Next circle I'll invite a few children to share a "best moment" rather than a result.

qa.q: Who actually scored the winning goal?
qa.a: Chaitanya said, "I scored it. Noor passed to me."

qa.q: What does Noor's answer about the pass suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Noor felt genuinely proud of her pass, and the bigger claim came from wanting to feel important in front of the class.

qa.q: How did the teacher support Noor?
qa.a: The teacher avoided shaming her in front of everyone, asked about her real best moment, and showed her that the pass was worth being proud of.

qa.q: How does Chaitanya see the moment when Noor claims the goal?
qa.a: Chaitanya feels he has to set the record straight, but he does it quietly, and he is pleased when Noor later praises his goal.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a child claiming the winning goal to win attention, a wish to matter rather than a plan to fool anyone.

passage:
Saturday, after the river picnic.
Today I, Mohit, caught a fish. A small silver one, about as long as my hand. Papa helped me pull it in and then we let it go.
When we got home, my cousin Mehak asked what happened, and I said, "I caught a fish as big as a dog!" Her mouth fell open. So I kept going. I said it pulled me into the water and I had to swim back. She asked me to tell it again at dinner. Everyone laughed and clapped.
It was the best feeling. Nobody ever listens to my stories like that.
But when Papa heard the dog part, he winked at me and said, "A small dog, maybe. A puppy." Everybody laughed again, and I laughed too. I wasn't trying to trick anyone. I just wanted it to be a big story.

qa.q: How long was the fish Mohit caught?
qa.a: It was about as long as Mohit's hand.

qa.q: Why did Mohit keep making the story bigger?
qa.a: Mohit felt thrilled that Mehak and everyone were listening, and wanted to feel important, since usually nobody listens to his stories like that.

qa.q: How did Papa handle the exaggeration kindly?
qa.a: Papa gently shrank the story with a joke about a puppy, so the truth came back without shaming Mohit.

qa.q: What is it like for Mehak to hear the fish story?
qa.a: Mehak feels amazed and excited, wanting to hear it again at dinner, because she believes the big version.

grounding: A child's diary shows a child stretching a fish story to win attention, as play and a wish to matter rather than a plan to fool.

passage:
At the village well after school in Khandala, Varun waved his arms. "I saw a hundred monkeys on the way! A HUNDRED! And the biggest one took my roti and I chased it all the way to the temple!"
The other children gasped. Little Pinky asked, "Were you scared?"
"No! I'm never scared."
His grandfather, Pradeep dada, sat on the charpai nearby, peeling peas. He smiled into his moustache. That morning Varun had come home and said there were four monkeys, and that he had hidden behind the gate.
Later, as they walked home, dada said, "A hundred monkeys, eh?"
Varun grinned. "Maybe four. But a hundred is a better story."
"It is," dada said. "Just tell me the four-monkey version when it's important. Like if one bites you."
Varun laughed and took his hand.

qa.q: How many monkeys did Varun tell his grandfather about that morning?
qa.a: Four monkeys.

qa.q: Why did Varun say he saw a hundred monkeys?
qa.a: Varun felt excited and wanted the other children to be impressed; a hundred simply made a better story.

qa.q: How did Pradeep dada handle the exaggeration?
qa.a: He smiled, asked gently about it on the walk home, and asked for the true version when it really matters, like a bite.

qa.q: How might the other children see Varun's story?
qa.a: They were thrilled and gasped, enjoying the adventure, without knowing it had grown from four monkeys.

grounding: Shows a child stretching a monkey story to excite friends and win attention, as play and a wish to matter rather than to fool anyone.
